overview.text: In geometry, a vertex (plural: vertices) is a point where sides or edges meet—the corner of a polygon or a solid. In graph theory, the same word names a dot representing an object; edges represent connections between objects, so a vertex can stand for, for example, an airport in a flight network. Unlike a polygon corner, a graph vertex need not be joined to any edge, and its location or the shape of the drawn edges does not determine the network: what matters is which vertices connect. Graph vertices are also called nodes. Thus, “vertex” links familiar geometric corners with a general way to describe structures and relationships.

key_facts.text: The plural of vertex is vertices.
A polygon’s corners and a solid’s corners are examples of geometric vertices.
In a graph, vertices represent objects and edges represent their connections.
A graph vertex can have degree zero: it may have no edges connected to it.
In graph theory, the arrangement or shape of the drawn edges can change without changing which vertices are connected.
